extracted.intended_audience: scientists, experimentalists, and students of the philosophy/methods of science
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological principles for evaluating scientific theories, designing experiments, and interpreting measurements—covering prediction (qualitative and quantitative), measurement practice, error analysis, and strategies of discovery (e.g., inversion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive power of theory (qualitative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory should predict phenomena — including novel or previously unobserved appearances — whose subsequent observation corroborates the theory (e.g., wave-interference effects in light and sound).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: interference predicted in light (Huyghens, Young, Fresnel) and sound (Herschel, Weber); successful observation (Lloyd, Professor Lloyd, Weber) removes doubt about the theory. Anti-pattern: failing to test novel, distinctive predictions that strongly differentiate theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive power of theory (quantitative)
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong test of theory is the ability not only to predict that a phenomenon will occur but to assign its precise numerical amount, which can later be measured and compared with the theoretical value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Calculate expected magnitudes (Newton's moon-fall example; Thomson's predictions about melting-point shifts and thermo-elastic effects). Verification increases confidence; discrepancies require re-examination of data or theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical measurement without theoretical connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Purely empirical measurements record quantities without being explained or connected theoretically; such isolated numbers have little scientific value unless reduced and compared with theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: large tables of observations in chemistry, meteorology, public observatories. Best practice: reduce and compare measurements with theoretical expectations; anti-pattern: merely accumulating numerical tables with no reduction or comparison (waste of labour and money).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory-indicated quantities measured empirically
rubrics_metrics.description: When theory indicates the existence (and often the period/character) of a small or complex quantitative effect but cannot assign its magnitude, targeted empirical measurements should be made to determine the amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: atmospheric tides—theory indicated existence and periods; method-of-means and carefully selected observation sites allowed detection of tiny effects (~0.003–0.004 inch). Use theory to choose when/where to measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the method of means / statistical separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect small effects by taking means of observations in conditions where the effect is present vs absent (or different phases), trusting that other casual effects average out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: select observations by theoretical criteria (e.g., moon on meridian vs horizon), compute means, take differences to isolate effect. Advantage: theory helps decide grouping to separate principal disturbing effects; can set up simultaneous mean equations to solve for multiple effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculate probable error; distinguish variable and fixed errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute the probable error of the mean of observed results to assess whether divergence between experiment and theory is within expected random variation; non-overlap indicates fixed (systematic) errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If theoretical result lies within limits of probable error and experimental results agree with each other, theory is supported. Probable error measures incidental/variable sources only; if means from two methods do not overlap, search for overlooked fixed causes of error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explained results vs. mere coincidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when measurements agree with theory, the coincidence may be accidental; the degree and variability of divergence should be examined to judge whether agreement genuinely supports the theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small, variable divergences are often due to minor experimental errors; compute probable error and compare. If agreement among experimental runs is comparable to agreement with theory, probability of theory increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect theoretical knowledge of unobservable phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory can legitimately assert the existence and characterize phenomena that cannot be observed directly (either because effects are too small or inherently unobservable), and give meaningful, sometimes precise, properties of such phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: systematic aberration due to solar motion, molecular velocities, refractive indices of metals, properties of ether. Such hypothetical determinations can be substantial scientific knowledge despite being unverifiable by direct observation in the present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion of cause and effect as an experimental strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: The inversion of cause and effect—using known antecedents and consequents to produce the inverse effect—serves as a fertile method of discovery and prediction (e.g., producing cold by allowing expansion, producing heat by stretching india-rubber).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Joule's demonstrations, freezing mixtures as inversion of melting, electrical and thermo-electric reciprocal relations (Faraday). Recommended practice: consider inverse processes when exploring phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical classification to plan experiments and predict novel entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification and manipulation of formulas and theoretical schemes allow the prediction of new substances or phenomena and guide experimental synthesis and discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mendeléeff's prediction of gallium and some properties; Williamson's predictions in organic chemistry; Cayley's combinatorial calculations of possible compounds. Use theory to design synthetic targets and experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of theory due to irregularities / complex boundary conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretical predictions may be limited or inapplicable when real-world irregularities (e.g., nonuniform sea depths, complex boundaries) introduce unknown quantities and complexities that theory cannot fully cope with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: tidal theory complicated by irregular sea forms—exact theoretical investigation only possible for idealized uniform ocean. Best practice: acknowledge limitations and seek approximate or empirical methods when full theory fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of reducing and comparing observational tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Observational data should be reduced and compared with theoretical expectations rather than left as isolated tables; without reduction and comparison the bulk of numerical records is of limited scientific value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good practice: institutions (e.g., Greenwich Observatory) should reduce observations and compare them with theoretical models to find errors or new phenomena; otherwise numerical compilation can be wasted effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory aids experimental design by indicating when disturbances are present
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory is valuable in experimental design because it tells when each principal disturbing effect is present or absent, allowing means to be drawn that separate distinct effects and reduce confounding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: drawing means that give sums of different subsets of effects yields simultaneous equations whose solution isolates each quantity. Use theoretical knowledge to stratify observations strategically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small and insensible phenomena pervade nature; measurements are aggregates
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed phenomena are often aggregates of innumerable minute changes; recognizing that many changes are below sensory/instrumental thresholds should inform experimental sensitivity and interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: infinitesimal temperature variations, innumerable minor planetary perturbations, tiny chemical/electric actions. Implication: design experiments considering that observable effects may be rare aggregates of ubiquitous micro-processes; consider instrument sensitivity and aggregation methods.
